query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, high-temperature stable anti-oxidation coating (such as an Al2O3-forming layer) on cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will significantly enhance its oxygen resistance during high-temperature exposure without degrading its inherent mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Deposit a uniform, adherent, high-temperature anti-oxidation coating (e.g., via aluminizing or physical vapor deposition to form an Al2O3-type layer) on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure to air at 1000 °C for durations representative of service (e.g., 24 hours) combined with mechanical loading at strain rates between 10^(-4) and 10^(-2) s^(-1) during high-temperature tensile testing.
generation.structural_mediator: The coherent oxide coating acts as a diffusion barrier, reducing oxygen ingress and the formation of detrimental oxides at the alloy surface and grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The coating prevents rapid oxygen uptake and subsequent oxidation embrittlement during high-temperature exposure, thereby preserving the alloy’s microstructural integrity and mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated alloy is expected to exhibit a substantial reduction in oxidation-induced degradation while maintaining yield strength and ductility comparable to the untreated state under high-temperature tensile conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, which shows poor oxygen resistance and oxidation-induced embrittlement at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness is evaluated under high-temperature (approximately 1000 °C) air exposure and tensile loading conditions specified above; the intervention’s performance outside these parameters remains to be tested.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties include the long-term adhesion and thermal compatibility of the coating with the substrate during thermal cycling, and whether any potential coating-induced residual stresses might subtly alter the mechanical properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set with the applied anti-oxidation coating (e.g., via aluminizing to form an Al2O3 scale) and one uncoated control group. Subject both sets to a high-temperature air exposure of 1000 °C for 24 hours. Following exposure, conduct tensile tests at strain rates of 10^(-4) to 10^(-2) s^(-1) to evaluate yield strength and ductility.
measurements: Weight gain or oxide scale thickness (to gauge oxidation extent)
Surface and cross-sectional microstructural analysis (by SEM/TEM) for oxidation-induced changes
Tensile yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation measurements at room and elevated temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples show similar or greater oxidation degradation (e.g., significant oxide scale development, deteriorated microstructure) and exhibit statistically lower yield strength or ductility compared to the uncoated control after high-temperature exposure, then the hypothesis—that the coating preserves mechanical performance by enhancing oxygen resistance—is falsified.

He defined high-entropy alloys (HEAs) as having five or more major elements beneath 5–35 at.%, and minor elements below five at.%. In 2006, he also established four core effects of HEAs []: High-entropy, severe-lattices-distortion, sluggish-diffusion, and the cocktail effect. With the new concepts, scientists are able to develop and expand alloys without restrictions [,,,,]. Some HEAs have been found to have attractive properties on diffusion [], oxidation [], corrosion [], fatigue [], creep [], fracture toughness [], and elevated-temperature strength []. High-entropy superalloys (HESAs) [], eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [], light-weight HEAs (LWHEAs) [], refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) [], etc. have been proposed and attract increased attention.
